extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of social science, political philosophy, and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological rules for producing and evaluating generalizations in social science and historical sociology, including how to derive empirical laws, connect them to human nature, and the requisites of stable political society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize from history without grounds in human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an imperative rule never to introduce any generalization from history into the social science unless sufficient grounds can be pointed out for it in human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical generalizations must be connected to psychological and ethological laws; otherwise they remain empirical and have limited predictive value. The text stresses this as a fundamental methodological rule and repeatedly warns against accepting empirical laws from history alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert empirical historical laws into scientific laws by consilience with laws of human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: An empirical law suggested by history can only be relied on for scientific prediction if it can be connected with the psychological and ethological laws on which it depends, converting it from an empirical law into a scientific one by deduction a priori with historical evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: M. Comte is singled out as an exception who recognized the necessity of connecting generalizations from history with laws of human nature. Without such consilience, generalizations are merely empirical and applicable only to adjacent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of treating observed historical sequences as laws of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of succession traced among different states of society could only be an empirical law unless connected to deeper laws of human nature; it cannot be assumed to be an independent law of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a regular order of succession observed in history remains empirical; the text warns that without theoretical grounding in human nature its predictive power is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require verification of empirical laws by psychological and ethological laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The only check or corrective on erroneous generalization from history is constant verification by psychological and ethological laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because few nations have reached high stages of independent development, empirical laws often rely on few instances; verifying them against fundamental laws of human nature reduces error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence requirement for preparing historical generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: No one but a person competently skilled in the laws of human nature is capable of preparing the materials for historical generalization by analyzing facts of history or observing social phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A competent analyst knows the comparative importance of different facts, what to observe, and how to infer facts that are not directly observable. Incompetent observers will misjudge evidence and produce erroneous generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish empirical laws of co-existence and of succession (social statics vs dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws of society are of two kinds: uniformities of co-existence (social statics) and uniformities of succession (social dynamics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social Statics: ascertains conditions of stability and mutual actions of contemporaneous phenomena, useful for inferring one element from another. Social Dynamics: theory of society in progressive movement, concerned with laws of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use statical (coexistence) analysis to infer conditions when direct observation is impracticable
rubrics_metrics.description: The statical view allows inference of characteristic marks of each social mode by treating elements in their mutual interdependence; it can supply the place of direct observation provisionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to anatomy: if the state of one well-marked division is known, one can infer the contemporaneous state of others by necessary correlation. But indirect exploration must be complemented by careful estimation of limits of variation to avoid error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid oversimplified necessary-relations claims among social elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessary relations among different aspects of society are not so simple and precise that observed results could only have arisen from a single mode of mutual coordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cautions against narrow notions that would claim unique coordination; instead one must estimate limits of variation in healthy and morbid states as complement to statical theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require multiple, well-analyzed instances before accepting empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws must be the result of more than a few instances; if one or two instances are insufficiently known or imperfectly analyzed, a wrong empirical law will emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because few nations have independently reached high social stages, reliance on few cases is hazardous. Thorough comparison and adequate analysis are necessary to avoid erroneous generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine statical and dynamical views to find laws of correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rest on noting progressive changes in separate elements alone; combine the statical view (contemporaneous condition) with the dynamical (progressive changes) to obtain empirically the law of correspondence between simultaneous states and simultaneous changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This law of correspondence, once verified a priori, would serve as the true scientific derivative law of development. The process requires difficult observation and comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek a pre-eminent social element as central chain when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: If some one element in social existence is pre-eminent as prime agent of social movement, take its progress as the central chain to which other progressions can be appended, simplifying the order of filiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text identifies the state of the speculative faculties (beliefs, knowledge) as such a pre-eminent element, with evidence from history showing intellectual change typically precedes other social changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize state of knowledge/speculative faculties as determinant of social progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The order of human progression mainly depends on the order of progression in the intellectual convictions of mankind — the law of successive transformations of human opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progress of knowledge limits industrial and artistic improvement; changes in prevalent beliefs often precede and cause large social changes. Thus studying changes in opinion is essential to explaining social dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limits of a priori deduction for long causal series
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not possible, setting out from principles of human nature and general circumstances, to determine a priori the full order in which human development must take place because of the long series of reactions and the amplification of small errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A slight error in any term of a long causal series grows rapidly; therefore empirical verification and historical evidence are indispensable for complex social sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take wide historical span into account for laws of opinion progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the progress of knowledge and changes in opinions manifest slowly over long intervals, one must consider the whole of past time from the first recorded conditions to present phenomena to determine the law of successive transformations of opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-term or partial historical samples are inadequate to establish broad empirical laws of intellectual development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat requisites of political stability as empirical regularities to be tested against human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain circumstances found in all societies that maintain collective existence (laws or equivalent usages, tribunals, organized executive force, public authorities) can be considered conditions of a State when psychological and ethological laws confirm the indication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are initially empirical findings from comparison of societies; some, when consistent with deeper laws of human nature, may be elevated to scientific truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education with restraining discipline as a condition of social union
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of education beginning in infancy and continued through life, with a main ingredient of restraining discipline to train habitually subordinating personal impulses to the ends of society, is a principal requisite of stable political society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives historical examples (ancient commonwealths, religious teaching in modern nations) and warns that relaxing restraining discipline correlates with disorganization and decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of allegiance/loyalty (a fixed, unquestioned point) as a condition of political permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be something in the constitution of the state 'settled, something permanent, and not to be called in question' — an object of allegiance or loyalty (gods, persons, laws, or principles) which anchors the social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fixed point can take different shapes but in durable societies it prevents conflicts from undermining the fundamental system; habitual questioning of those fundamentals leads to near-constant civil strife.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of cohesion (sympathy/common interest) as essential to unity
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong and active principle of cohesion among members of the same community — sympathy and feeling of common interest — is essential; not a vulgar nationalism but a sense of being one people sharing common fate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts productive cohesion in great commonwealths with absence of nationality causing weakness (examples: Rome, England/Ireland, Italy, Austrian empire, South America). Cohesion prevents fragmentation and secessionist tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy and necessary correlations among sciences/arts to infer social conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a necessary relation between the condition of the sciences in general and that of the arts in general, and more generally among different branches such that knowledge of one can enable inference about others by their necessary correlation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The history of sciences provides examples (e.g., connection between general state of astronomy and geometry) showing how indirect inference can expose false claims about historical attainments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize empirical laws have limited scope without a priori grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical generalizations from history are applicable only within bounds of actual observation and cannot determine their real limits or whether changes will continue, terminate, or reverse without connection to a priori principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore, social science must aim to convert empirical laws into derivative laws connected to elementary laws of human nature to achieve scientific status and predictive usefulness.
